SpaceVision 2026 Business Pitch Competition

Coldtrap

The Moon's ice is poisoned. We clean it, and the poison builds the base.

Arnav Rai, University of Chicago · UChicago Space Program (SEDS)
Challenge category: oxygen production, with advanced materials as the secondary category.

Behind this text: a permanently shadowed polar crater. The Sun sits on the horizon, so the rim is lit and the floor has not seen daylight in two billion years.left click: next · right click: back
0:00–0:45. Open on the hook, no self-intro first. "Everybody here wants to mine the Moon's ice. Almost nobody talks about what's in it." Then name yourself and the company, and say the category out loud. The crater behind you is the whole business: lit rim, dark floor, and a cable between them.

The rim sees the Sun all day. The floor has never seen it.

At the pole the Sun circles the horizon instead of rising. Over one lunar day the rim is lit from every direction and the bowl stays black. That is why the ice is still there, and why the floor sits near 40 K.

The ice everyone wants to mine is dirty

What the floor of Cabeus contained when LCROSS hit it in 2009, by weight. One impact site, so these are first estimates.

5.5% waterThe prize everyone is after
1.74% hydrogen sulfideA third as much poison gas as water
0.31% ammoniaPlus methane, sulfur dioxide, methanol, CO₂
CO, H₂, and mercuryMercury and silver were seen in the same plume

Sulfides poison electrolyzers

Oxygen plants split water over catalysts. Sulfur compounds bind to them and kill the plant.

Mercury makes it undrinkable

Any water for crews must be stripped of heavy metals to parts-per-billion levels.

Nobody has done this on the Moon

Earth purification plants are heavy, power-hungry, and not built for abrasive regolith or one-sixth gravity.

The crater does the separating

Mined ice is warmed in a sealed cell. The vapor rises past cold plates that sit at different heights above the 40 K floor, so each gas freezes onto its own plate. The refinery only ever adds heat. Each click lowers the temperature.

click to lower the temperature
250K at the top plate

Freeze-out temperatures are approximate cold-trap stability values for lunar vacuum (Zhang & Paige, 2009). Illustrative, not a process simulation.

4:30–5:40. Drag the slider yourself, slowly. Water freezes onto the top plate first near 110 K, then methanol and mercury, ammonia near 65 K, sulfur dioxide, CO₂, hydrogen sulfide near 50 K, and the light gases last. "On Earth this separation needs refrigeration plants. Here the refrigerator is the crater."

5:40–6:30. Read it as a story: everything that makes the ice unusable becomes something the base would otherwise import at a million dollars a kilogram. Then the per-tonne numbers, which show you've done the mass balance.

The chemistry is a century old. The location is new.

Poison to sulfur: the Claus process

2 H₂S + O₂ → 2 S + 2 H₂O

Run in every oil refinery since the 1880s. We spend a little of our own oxygen and get back sulfur and extra water. Reaction heat helps keep the refinery warm.

Water to air and fuel

2 H₂O → 2 H₂ + O₂

Standard electrolysis, powered by day. At night the gases run back through fuel cells, so the oxygen plant doubles as the base's battery and the tanks are the oxygen reserve.

Sulfur to concrete

35% sulfur + 65% regolith, 140 °C

NASA Marshall tests: about 34 MPa compressive strength, with no water and no curing time. It sets as it cools. Our fabric mold seals it from vacuum, where exposed sulfur would slowly sublime.

Ammonia to air and food

4 NH₃ + 3 O₂ → 2 N₂ + 6 H₂O

Burning ammonia gives nitrogen buffer gas for habitat air. Oxidizing it to nitrate instead gives the fertilizer hydroponic crops prefer. Either way the Moon's only nitrogen source becomes usable.

Toutanji & Grugel, NASA Marshall 2008; Omar & Issa, ASCE Space '94; Grugel & Toutanji, Adv. Space Res. 2008 (sublimation concerns)Coldtrap
6:30–7:10. This is the technology-score slide: nothing here is new chemistry, and that's the point. Judges score "relies on existing technology" highly. Spend 30 seconds, not more.

A folding mold that becomes a shield

cutaway view
click to unfold the shelter

Ships flat. A double-walled fabric shell, folded into a lander.

Meters show the direction of each layer's effect, not a dose calculation.

7:10–8:10. Click through the layers while you talk. The fabric skins are the mold; robots pump hot sulfur-regolith between them; it sets without curing or water; the skins seal the sulfur from vacuum. The water lining is better cosmic-ray shielding per kilogram than rock, because hydrogen stops heavy nuclei without the secondary showers rock produces, and it doubles as the emergency reserve: the rubric's "backup systems" line. Water expands when it freezes, so the lining holds ice on purpose or uses bladders with room to expand.

Why the water lining matters: rock makes showers, water doesn't

cosmic-ray bursts every few seconds

Galactic cosmic rays are heavy nuclei moving near light speed. Hitting the silicon and iron in regolith, they shatter into secondary particles that keep going. Hydrogen in water breaks them up with far fewer secondaries. Same thickness, different result.

0particles through the regolith slab
0particles through the water slab

Illustrative animation of the secondary-shower effect, not a transport calculation. The physics: NASA's radiation shielding work favors hydrogen-rich materials (water, polyethylene) over equal mass of regolith for galactic cosmic rays; regolith remains excellent against solar storms. That is why the shelter uses both.

8:10–8:40. Fire one burst and let it run. "Both slabs are the same thickness. Rock turns one particle into many. Water doesn't. That is why NASA shields with water and polyethylene, and why the lining inside our regolith wall is water we make on site."

What is new, and what we deliberately buy

Coldtrap owns
  • Sulfur from the ice. Every lunar sulfur-concrete study assumes mining troilite rock and reducing it. We take the sulfur out of the ice's worst contaminant, where it already is.
  • The sealed fabric mold. A folding shelter that is its own formwork and seals the sulfur from vacuum, answering the one objection materials researchers raise about sulfur concrete.
  • Cold-driven separation. Staged cold plates above a 40 K floor, so the plant never needs a refrigerator, only heaters.
  • The loop. One site producing water, oxygen, night power, nitrogen, fertilizer, and shelter, with the shield doubling as the reserve.
bought or licensed
  • Rim power: Blue Origin Power Tower, Astrobotic VSAT, and NASA's fission reactor in the 2030s
  • Superconducting cable: UChicago PME (Prof. Shuolong Yang, NASA Early Career Faculty award) and Michigan Tech's T-REX tether deployment
  • Electrolyzers, fuel cells, and excavation robots, all off the shelf
  • Delivery on CLPS landers; later Blue Moon or Starship cargo

Buying these keeps our capital in the parts nobody else makes, and turns likely competitors into suppliers.

8:10–8:40. The originality slide. Be candid: the parts exist, the link doesn't. If a judge knows about T-REX or the UChicago cable, agree enthusiastically; they are partners on slide 5.

one pilot year, illustrative

Processing 2,000 tonnes of crater material (about 5.5 tonnes a day, a small excavator's pace) yields roughly:

  • 110 t water → ~95 t oxygen-equivalent, 5 t nitrogen-equivalent demand covered many times over
  • 32 t sulfur → ~90 t sulfur concrete, four shelter shells
  • 5 t nitrogen → air for a 4-module habitat with years of leakage margin

Selling even 20 tonnes of water and oxygen in year one at target prices clears $3–4B of avoided import cost for NASA and tens of millions in revenue for Coldtrap. Numbers scale with how dirty and how rich the ice turns out to be.

What could go wrong, what we do about it, and what backs it up

Nobody has measured the ice in placeThe 2025 drill meant to settle it tipped over. Phase 1 is sized as a pilot and doubles as the measurement; its data is a product NASA will pay for.
Sulfur concrete weakens under temperature swingsOur shell is sealed inside fabric and buried under regolith, which holds it at far steadier temperatures than exposed surfaces see.
Storing energy as hydrogen and oxygen is inefficientRound trip is 30–50%. We sell resilience through the 14-day night, not efficiency, and the same tanks are the oxygen supply.
Early dependence on one customerNASA carries Phase 1, as it did for every lander company. Phases 2 and 3 move to leases and commercial oxygen buyers.
The sunlit stretch of cable needs coolingOnly the rim segment; the crater does the rest. Our partners' tether designs already plan a short conventional section.
Dust and cold kill machinery on the floorThe refinery sits inside its own sulfur-shell shelter, the first thing we build, and runs warm on its own reaction heat.
backup powerStored hydrogen and oxygen run fuel cells if the rim towers or the reactor drop out; one cable takes both sources.
backup water and airThe shelters' water lining is tonnes of reserve water and oxygen, already next to the crew.
backup feedstockIf one crater's ice disappoints, the same plant moves: it is sized as a single CLPS-class payload.
backup revenuePhase 1 sells data and clean water even at low ice yields; Phase 2 shelters sell without any ice at all.
Keep for Q&A if time is short. Say these before the judges do; the rubric rewards roadblocks considered. The ice-uncertainty answer is the important one: the pilot is also the prospecting mission.

End on the line, then stop and invite questions. If the ask size is challenged: it is sized to an SBIR Phase II plus matching, and the prototype generates the data that unlocks a Tipping Point award. Appendix slides follow for Q&A.
appendix · for questions

Why the crater is the right factory

Cold enough for free superconductors

Shadowed floors sit at about 40–60 K. The standard YBCO superconductor works below 91 K, so a cable laid on the floor needs no cooling. NASA's own planning lists a possible need for 10 kW, 5 km superconducting cables in these regions.

Cold enough to store cryogens

Liquid oxygen boils at 90 K and freezes at 54 K; the floor is colder than both, so oxygen storage needs a little heat, not refrigeration. Hydrogen (20 K) still needs a small cooler, far smaller than anywhere else.

Warm enough to run

The refinery's Claus reaction and fuel cells release heat. Inside its sulfur-shell shelter the plant stays in the 250–300 K band electronics like, while its cold plates reach into the 40 K environment outside.

Power on the rim

Ridges within 15 km of the pole are lit up to ~90% of the year. Two points 8 km apart on the Shackleton ridge are lit a combined ~94%. Towers there are the near-term supply; a 40 kW reactor follows.

Night survival solved by design

Stored hydrogen and oxygen run fuel cells through the 14-day night; the shelters' regolith and water walls hold heat. The base's reserves are the same tanks the refinery fills by day.

Why water beats rock for radiation

Galactic cosmic rays are heavy, fast nuclei. Striking silicon and iron in regolith they shatter into secondary showers. Hydrogen-rich water breaks them up with far fewer secondaries, which is why NASA shields with water and polyethylene.
